articles.title: NeoSyntropy documentation
articles.description: Build controlled AI workflows as explicit graphs. Models propose the next step; the control layer decides what is allowed to happen.

sections.title: A control layer for model-driven systems
paragraphs: NeoSyntropy separates probabilistic decisions from deterministic control. Models can propose what should happen next; a finite-state graph defines what is allowed to happen.

You author nodes and edges in the Python SDK. When backend credentials are set, the NeoSyntropy backend owns selection, routing, plan validation, and state commits. The client only executes local handlers and submits results.

cards.title: Explicit graph
cards.text: Nodes describe capabilities. Edges describe permitted movement.

cards.title: Fail-closed gates
cards.text: Transition legality and guards reject illegal steps before commit.

cards.title: Typed tools
cards.text: Nodes declare allow-listed tools with pydantic schemas; undeclared calls never run.

sections.title: Two execution modes
paragraphs: With backend credentials, ControlManager runs an opaque execute/commit loop against POST /api/v1/control/runs. Without credentials, the SDK falls back to a local deterministic router for offline development.

callout.title: Preferred path
callout.text: Use BackendClient + ControlManager for production. Prefer the control API over internal /api/v1/framework/* inference endpoints.

articles.title: Run a controlled workflow
articles.description: Install the Python SDK, define a small graph, and run it through the backend-owned control cycle.

sections.title: 1. Install the SDK
paragraphs: Install the neosyntropy package from the framework repository (or your package index when published).

pip install -e .
# or: pip install neosyntropy

sections.title: 2. Set credentials
paragraphs: Point the SDK at the NeoSyntropy API. Use an API key with the framework:invoke scope, or a user access token with an active subscription.

sections.title: 3. Define a graph and run

code.label: Python

paragraphs: ControlManager discovers credentials from the environment when backend is omitted. Every cycle returns a RunResult with an AuditRecord of proposals, gate checks, and committed transitions.

articles.title: What NeoSyntropy controls
articles.description: A model may propose a bounded plan; the runtime checks that plan against graph structure and transition legality before anything commits.

sections.title: Proposal is not permission
paragraphs: The router does not perform business operations. It proposes candidate nodes and an execution topology. Validators and the transition table decide whether that proposal may run and whether state may advance.
This keeps language-model judgment useful without making model output the final authority for state movement or side effects.

cards.title: Selection
cards.text: Retrieve and rank likely capabilities for the current intent and state.

cards.title: Control
cards.text: Validate topology, prerequisites, fallback isolation, and edges.

cards.title: Execution
cards.text: Run local handlers (or provider-backed nodes), then submit results for commit.

sections.title: Python SDK entry point
paragraphs: The public control surface is ControlManager. With a BackendClient it starts an opaque control run, executes local work units, and submits results until the backend completes or rejects the cycle.

code.label: Python SDK
code.code:
from neosyntropy import ControlManager, FSM

manager = ControlManager(graph)  # BackendClient.from_env() when credentials exist
result = manager.run({
    "intent": "verify the customer and review refund eligibility",
    "current_state": "Start",
    "state": {"order_id": "ord_123"},
})

print(result.final_state)
print(result.completed)
print(result.rejected)

articles.title: Nodes are executable capabilities
articles.description: A node packages one capability the router can select. Nodes are not workflow positions.

sections.title: What belongs in a node
paragraphs: A node packages a Python handler or a provider-backed prompt, declared tools, prerequisites, an optional group, and an optional fallback marker.
Nodes return a NodeResult — output, state_updates, and an optional next_state. That result is a proposal. Nothing a node returns commits state by itself.

sections.title: The router selects nodes
paragraphs: The backend ranks candidates and proposes one or more nodes arranged as parallel, sequential, hybrid, or fallback execution.
Selecting two nodes does not create two current states. A workflow instance still has one current state, and any state change is committed only after gates pass.

code.label: Python SDK

sections.title: Tools live on nodes
paragraphs: Tools are capabilities on a node (tools=("lookup_order",)), never graph vertices. Handlers call them through a bound facade that enforces the allow-list fail-closed. Undeclared tool calls are denied fail-closed, not retries.

articles.title: Groups organize nodes
articles.description: A group is a named collection of nodes. It can also author an internal subgraph (nodes, routers, entry, edges) that compiles into the parent FSM. ControlManager still owns routing, validation, and state.

sections.title: Organization, with optional authored flow
paragraphs: Groups name collections of nodes for organization and candidate metadata. A semantic edge may target a group to scope routing; when entry is set, entering the group lands on that entry state.
Authoring helpers (@group.node, routers, entry, add_edge) compile into the parent FSM. They do not create a second control path — one pipeline owns the sequence end to end.

code.label: Python SDK

callout.title: See Control manager
callout.text: Regardless of how many groups a project contains, ControlManager owns select → route → validate → execute → commit.

articles.title: Edges define legal movement
articles.description: Nodes perform work; edges define which state-to-state movements are legal.

sections.title: State transitions
paragraphs: An edge connects one state to another. A node result may propose a target state; only a listed edge (or allow_unlisted_transitions=True) permits the move.
Edges carry labels with a fixed priority order that drives the deterministic preferred-path router, and optional guards — callables over state that gate the edge at runtime. Guards fail closed.

code.label: Python SDK

sections.title: When edges are not listed
paragraphs: Missing edges do not skip selection. Search still finds relevant nodes; validation fail-closes unless the hop is listed or the graph explicitly allows unlisted transitions.

callout.title: Search is not permission
callout.text: Node search answers relevance. Edges answer legality. A high-scoring node still cannot advance state without a legal transition.

articles.title: ControlManager owns the cycle
articles.description: One object runs select → route → validate → gate → execute → gate → commit → audit.

sections.title: Nodes are selected; state is advanced
paragraphs: The control layer can select multiple nodes because capabilities may run in parallel or sequence. It does not select multiple states.
After selected nodes finish, results propose state updates. Gates check legality; the backend commits at most one transition per step.

callout.title: Architectural boundary
callout.text: Node selection answers “what work should run?” State transition answers “where is the workflow now?” Keeping these decisions separate prevents execution topology from becoming workflow state.

sections.title: Control flow

code.label: Pipeline
code.code:
input -> candidate selection -> router proposal -> plan validation
      -> execution -> guards / transition checks -> one state commit
      -> audit record

bullets: Proposal is not permission — validators and the transition table decide.
Exactly one current state; at most one commit per plan step.
Fail-closed gates before commit, even after successful execution.
Every graph has exactly one dedicated fallback node.

sections.title: Backend-owned control (preferred)
paragraphs: When BackendClient credentials are configured, the backend owns selection, routing, validation, and commits. The client receives opaque execute steps (node ids only), runs local handlers, and posts results. Responses never include topology, candidates, scores, providers, or model names.

code.label: Remote loop
code.code:
POST /api/v1/control/runs
  <- status=awaiting_execution, step.nodes=[...]
execute local handlers
POST /api/v1/control/runs/{run_id}/results
  <- next step | completed | rejected

sections.title: Offline fallback
paragraphs: Without backend credentials, ControlManager uses DeterministicRouter locally: walk outgoing edges by label priority, or propose the dedicated fallback when nothing is legal.

articles.title: Backend control API
articles.description: Opaque execute/commit loop for framework workflows. Prefer this surface over internal framework inference endpoints.

sections.title: What the API exposes
paragraphs: The control API starts a backend-owned cycle and returns only client-visible fields: run status, current state, opaque execute steps, committed transitions, and rejection reasons.
It never returns topology, candidates, scores, providers, model names, or execution plans.

cards.title: User JWT
cards.text: Authorization: Bearer <access_token> with an active subscription.

cards.title: API key
cards.text: Authorization: Bearer nsk_... with scope framework:invoke and an active subscription.

cards.title: POST /api/v1/control/runs
cards.text: Start a control run with a graph manifest and request context.

cards.title: POST /api/v1/control/runs/{run_id}/results
cards.text: Submit local node results or a client_rejection; receive the next step or terminal status.

cards.title: GET /api/v1/control/runs/{run_id}
cards.text: Poll client-visible run status. Sessions are in-memory with a one-hour TTL.

sections.title: Start a run
paragraphs: Send a schema_version 1 graph manifest (nodes, edges, allow_unlisted_transitions) plus request context. Graphs require unique node ids and exactly one is_fallback: true node.

code.label: Request

sections.title: Submit results
paragraphs: Cover exactly the pending step.nodes with results, or send client_rejection (string ≤ 2000). The backend merges state, checks transition legality, commits at most one transition per step, and returns the next view.

code.label: Request

sections.title: SDK path (preferred)
paragraphs: Most applications should use BackendClient and ControlManager instead of calling the HTTP loop directly. The SDK builds the control graph manifest, runs local handlers, and submits wired NodeResults.

callout.title: Internal endpoints
callout.text: POST /api/v1/framework/semantic-node-hybrid, /router, and /slm power the control engine and generation. They are not the integration surface for application clients.

articles.title: Configure the SDK client
articles.description: Client configuration is environment-driven. Router, hybrid search, and SLM URLs are server-side only.

cards.title: NEOSYNTROPY_API_URL
cards.text: Base API URL. The SDK normalizes to …/api/v1.

cards.title: NEOSYNTROPY_API_KEY
cards.text: nsk_… key with framework:invoke (and telemetry:write for observers).

cards.title: NEOSYNTROPY_PROJECT_ID
cards.text: Sent as X-NeoSyntropy-Project-ID for project-scoped telemetry.

cards.title: NEOSYNTROPY_ACCESS_TOKEN
cards.text: Alternative to API key for user JWT auth.

sections.title: Server-side (not client-facing)
paragraphs: FRAMEWORK_ROUTER_*, FRAMEWORK_SEMANTIC_NODE_HYBRID_*, and FRAMEWORK_SLM_* configure upstream inference services on the backend. Application clients do not set these.
